title: Full Stack Developer
desc:
As the sole developer, I led the complete rebuild of the company's website, migrating from a legacy WordPress site to a modern Next.js 15 and React 19 build, owning the project end to end across design, frontend, backend, and deployment.

The rebuild was judged on outcomes, not tech. Web-form enquiries roughly doubled year over year and the on-site conversion rate more than doubled, from about 1.3% to about 3.0%, adding up to around 1,300 genuine enquiries in the first year. I carried search rankings through the migration and grew organic clicks around 3x in the most recent quarter, and made the site citeable by AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude. Along the way, reconciling conversions against the database exposed that analytics had been under-reporting them by around 40%, giving the business an accurate view of real demand for the first time.

caseStudies.tagline: Sole developer on a full migration from a legacy WordPress site to a Next.js 15 / React 19 rebuild, owned across design, frontend, backend, and deployment.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: The legacy WordPress site read as a set of disconnected templates, converted poorly, and gave the business no reliable picture of where its enquiries came from. I owned the rebuild end to end, and treated it as a product problem rather than a redesign: make the site convert, make it rank, and make every result measurable.

sections.heading: A design system, not just pages
sections.body: Rather than restyle pages one by one, I built a documented design system covering the brand's colour, motion, and typography, its CTA hierarchy, and its section and surface patterns, then rebuilt every page against it. New pages now look on-brand by default, and the site reads as one coherent premium product. I also separated all copy and listings from the components that render them, so the client's team can edit text or add a bar without touching code or breaking the design, keeping the site cheap to maintain long after handover.

sections.heading: Turning visits into enquiries
sections.body: The old contact form was a black box: enquiries arrived as unstructured emails with no record of which channel produced them. I rebuilt it into a validated, spam-resistant enquiry flow that captures each lead's event details and traffic source, stores every submission reliably, and notifies the team instantly. Web-form enquiries roughly doubled year over year and the on-site conversion rate more than doubled, from about 1.3% to about 3.0%. Reconciling the stored records against Google Analytics then revealed the dashboard was under-counting conversions by around 40% because of ad-blocking and consent loss, so for the first time the business could see true demand: about 1,300 genuine web-form enquiries in year one, with phone and WhatsApp on top.

sections.heading: Protecting rankings, then growing them
sections.body: A WordPress-to-Next.js migration can wipe out years of search equity overnight. I mapped 118 legacy URLs to their new homes so rankings carried across, and in the most recent quarter Google Search Console shows organic clicks up around 3x year over year and impressions around 2x, with average position improved from about 33 to about 20 (mobile from 35 to 12). The structured data I implemented put recipe and review rich results into Google where there were none before.

sections.heading: An early bet on AI search
sections.body: I added an llms.txt and LLM-readable markup so AI assistants can read and cite the site, then verified the payoff at the database level: 25 enquiries came directly from ChatGPT and Claude, a channel Google Analytics had logged as just 17 sessions. Measuring conversions against server-side records, rather than trusting the dashboard, is what turned AI search from a guess into a proven acquisition channel.

sections.heading: The problem — a business run by hand
sections.body: The Cocktail Lab ran on paper and disconnected tools. Enquiries were copied onto paper; quotes were worked out on a calculator and typed number-by-number into an email; invoices were hand-built in Zoho; the registration form lived in SharePoint; and picking relied on a recipe tool that was not connected to stock — it listed generic ingredients like 'vodka 500ml', so pickers did not know which of many bottles to pull and had no stock visibility, leading to last-minute panic buying on the event day. Worst of all, sales and logistics worked off different systems that never talked: when a menu, guest count, or event time changed in SharePoint, the warehouse never heard about it.

sections.heading: The process — no PM, no spec, just the people doing the work
sections.body: With no product manager or analyst, I sat with the sales lead, the warehouse lead, and the owner and had them walk me through how the business actually ran. From those conversations I mapped the real workflow and picked out the steps worth automating or moving into a system. I treated it as a solutions-architecture problem: translate a paper-and-calculator workflow into one coherent system, owned end to end from requirements to production.

sections.heading: The solution — one pipeline, enquiry to delivery
sections.body: I built two custom Odoo modules (~10k lines) that form a single pipeline. A website enquiry now arrives over XML-RPC as a structured CRM lead — event date, guests, postcode, service type, and UTM attribution all mapped automatically, and designed lead-first so a slow or unavailable ERP never costs a lead. From there a quotation builder generates multi-package quotes from live product pricing, with no hardcoded rates, that customers accept through a portal. A stock-aware picking engine then turns each event's menu and bar setup into a real picking list against actual inventory, with unit conversion and serial and expiry tracking, so pickers pull specific bottles instead of guessing. Because everything lives in one system, a change sales makes to a menu or time propagates to the warehouse automatically — the silo is gone. It is self-hosted on Docker with matched production and development environments.

sections.heading: The result
sections.body: The business went from five disconnected manual tools to one system that carries an event from web enquiry to delivery. Sales and logistics finally share a single source of truth, quotes come from live pricing instead of a calculator, and inventory-aware picking removed the event-day scramble. Operational metrics — quote turnaround, panic-buy reduction, events per month — are still being measured, and are kept qualitative here until there are numbers I can stand behind.

title: Full Stack Web Developer
desc: At Joseph and Stacey, I contributed as a Full-Stack Developer, building and maintaining ERP and e-commerce systems using Svelte and Ruby. I worked closely with cross-functional teams to design user-centric interfaces, optimize database structures, and implement solutions that enhanced operational efficiency and system reliability. This experience sharpened my ability to adapt quickly, solve complex problems, and deliver meaningful results.

title: Java Back-End School 2nd
desc: This bootcamp was focused on modern web development practices and advanced tools. I deepened my knowledge of backend development by learning Spring Security for authentication and authorization, JPA for data management, and JUnit for testing. I also gained hands-on experience with JWT for secure communication and Swagger for automated API documentation. The course included server-side rendering with Thymeleaf and introduced me to containerized deployment using Docker and Kubernetes, as well as cloud environment management with AWS EC2. Additionally, I learned how to test APIs using Postman and streamline the build process with Gradle. This program helped me strengthen my skills with cutting-edge technologies and efficient workflows.

title: Java Full Stack Bootcamp Course
desc: During this bootcamp, I gained a solid foundation in web development. I learned to build backend logic using Java and the Spring Framework, integrating databases with MyBatis and Oracle. On the frontend, I used JSP, jQuery, and Ajax to create dynamic and interactive user interfaces, along with Bootstrap for responsive design. The program also introduced me to deploying applications on AWS RDS and Heroku, while managing development environments with Apache Tomcat and Maven. This course provided a comprehensive understanding of the web development process, with a focus on traditional and widely-used technologies.
